title: Federal Judges Question Trump Administration Compliance With Court Orders
description_short: Federal Judges Question Trump Administration Compliance With Court Orders
description_medium: By mid-March 2025, several federal judges had questioned whether the Trump administration was fully complying with court orders in cases involving deportations, federal employment, spending, and foreign aid, while the administration disputed allegations of noncompliance. In April, Judge James Boasberg found probable cause to hold officials in criminal contempt over the administration's handling of a March 15 order blocking Alien Enemies Act deportations. The evidence supports specific, case-by-case compliance disputes rather than a single blanket refusal to obey all injunctions.
description_long: By mid-March 2025, federal judges in several cases had questioned whether administration officials were complying fully with court orders. The supplied review identifies disputes involving deportations, federal employment, spending and foreign aid, while noting that the administration contested allegations of noncompliance. In April, Judge James Boasberg found probable cause to hold officials in criminal contempt concerning their handling of his March 15 order blocking Alien Enemies Act deportations. A probable-cause finding in that specific proceeding is different from a final contempt judgment in every other policy dispute. The earlier account merged the chronology and asserted that multiple judges had already held the administration in contempt by March 15. The supplied correction does not establish that assertion. The supported event is a set of identifiable compliance disputes and a later finding in the deportation case. Its institutional significance concerns the enforceability of judicial orders, but the evidence must still be presented case by case rather than as a blanket refusal to obey all injunctions.
